title: How does sealing improve `instanceof` checks and exhaustive `switch` pattern matching?
shortTitle: How does sealing improve `instanceof` checks and exhaustive `switch` pattern matching?
keyPoints: Sealing gives the compiler the complete, finite list of permitted subtypes so it can check exhaustiveness.
An exhaustive switch over a sealed type needs no default branch because every possible subtype is covered.
If a new subtype is added to the sealed type, every non-exhaustive switch fails to compile, catching gaps at compile time.
Adding a default branch to a sealed switch defeats the safety because it silently absorbs new subtypes.
Pattern matching with sealed types lets you test and destructure in one step using record patterns.
Multi-level sealed hierarchies are expanded transitively for exhaustiveness checking.

s1_definition.oneliner: Sealing makes the subtype set finite and known, so the compiler can prove a switch is exhaustive and force you to handle every case without a default.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Sealed type** – restricts which classes may extend it; the compiler knows the complete, finite set of subtypes.
- **Exhaustiveness checking** – the compiler verifies every permitted subtype is covered in a `switch`; no `default` needed.
- **Compile-time safety** – adding a new subtype causes every incomplete `switch` to fail compilation, not silently fall through.
- **Pattern matching** – `switch` patterns test type and bind variables in one step; record patterns destructure components.
- **No default rule** – deliberately omit `default` on sealed switches to keep the compile-time safety net.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has a fixed, closed list of exactly three account products. Because the list is closed, a clerk can write a checklist with one row per product and be certain it is complete. If head office later adds a fourth product, every incomplete checklist is immediately flagged. Sealing is what makes the list closed, so checklists can be provably complete.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Before Sealing (open hierarchy):

  TransactionResult (interface)
       │
       ├── Approved
       ├── Declined
       ├── Pending
       └── ??? (anyone can add)

  switch needs default → new subtypes silently absorbed

  After Sealing (closed hierarchy):

  sealed TransactionResult permits Approved, Declined, Pending
       │
       ├── Approved  (final record)
       ├── Declined  (final record)
       └── Pending   (final record)

  switch is exhaustive → no default
  Add new subtype → compiler error at every incomplete switch
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Sealing gives the compiler complete knowledge of the finite set of subtypes. Before sealed types, a `switch` or `instanceof` chain always needed a `default` to handle unknown subtypes, and that `default` silently swallowed any new subtype, causing runtime bugs. With sealing, the compiler checks exhaustiveness: a `switch` with a case for each permitted subtype is provably complete and needs no `default`.

The real power shows when the set changes. Adding a new permitted subtype causes every non-exhaustive `switch` to fail compilation. This turns a dangerous runtime gap into a compile-time error. In banking, where forgetting to handle a new transaction state could cause financial errors, this guarantee is enormously valuable.

Record patterns make it better still. You bind components directly in each case, extracting the amount from an approval or the reason from a decline without any cast. Guarded patterns with `when` let you refine within the closed set, like routing high-value approvals to compliance.

At National Bank of India, Pankaj modeled transaction results as a sealed interface with `Approved`, `Declined`, and `Pending` record subtypes. The dispatcher switches over all three with no `default`. When a teammate later added `Reversed`, the compiler pointed to every switch that needed updating. That is why you deliberately omit `default` on sealed switches: adding one would hide the safety net.

Remember one sentence: sealing closes the subtype set so the compiler can prove a switch is exhaustive, and adding a new subtype fails compilation everywhere it is not handled.
